title: Increasing writing output for German students
author: Special Education Today
summary: This post walks through a newly published single-case study by Noan Bräuer (University of Cologne) testing whether a package of explicit timing, immediate feedback, and positive reinforcement increased the number of words six German elementary students with reading and writing difficulties produced in essays. The blogger reports that results were modest and uneven across the six participants: clearly positive for one student, ambiguous or possibly just normal variation for two others. The piece's real argument is methodological caution: it pushes back against jumping from specific measured behaviors (word counts under an ABA design) to sweeping claims about abstract constructs like 'motivation,' and against treating any single small study as a definitive verdict on whether an intervention 'works.' The author frames the study as a valuable but limited data point that should sit inside a much larger, still-developing evidence base on writing interventions for struggling students.
points: Read single-case (ABA-design) studies for what they actually measured, not the broader psychological label ('motivation') often attached to the results afterward.

Treat this study's 'mostly higher values during the intervention phase' as modest, mixed evidence, strong for one student, ambiguous for others, rather than a general endorsement of the reinforcement package.
Avoid over-generalizing from a single small study (six students) to sweeping claims about whether reinforcement 'works' for writing instruction.
Value replication and a broad literature base over any single study when deciding whether to adopt an intervention like explicit timing plus feedback and reinforcement for struggling writers.
quotes: This single-case study, employing an ABA design, examined the effect of combined motivational methods on the length of stories written by six elementary school students with reading and writing difficulties.
The intervention comprised explicit timing, immediate feedback, and positive reinforcement.
I see these changes as modest. The differences between the A, B, and A phases for Pascal look good.
I am a bit reluctant to go up the scale or hierarchy of ideas from the actual measurement procedures and the manipulation of the variables to higher-order concepts like “motivation.
The study is simply an analysis of what happened under these conditions at this time with these student sand teacher. That is, in and of itself, valuable.
